Should you migrate from WordPress to Webflow?

A migration should improve how your website works, how your team publishes and how you serve your customers. Here are the questions to answer before changing platforms.

In this article

  1. 1. Start with the problem, then evaluate the platform
  2. 2. When Webflow is worth considering
  3. 3. When keeping WordPress may be the better decision
  4. 4. Compare everyday work and the total cost
  5. 5. A migration does not guarantee better SEO
  6. 6. Gather these five things before deciding
  7. Frequently asked questions
  8. References and further reading
Discuss my website →

1. Start with the problem, then evaluate the platform

If your website is hard to update, slow or visually inconsistent, changing platforms can feel like the obvious answer. First, identify the cause. Unsuitable hosting, oversized images or a poorly implemented design can also be addressed within WordPress.

My recommendation is to write down three specific problems and what would count as solving them. “The team needs to publish a case study without breaking the layout” is a useful objective. “We want a more modern platform” does not yet define the project.

The question behind the decision

What do we need to do better, and what will we have to rebuild to get there? If you cannot answer both parts, the site still needs a review.

2. When Webflow is worth considering

Webflow deserves an evaluation when your website mainly supports marketing: presenting services, showing projects, publishing articles and generating inquiries. It can be a useful choice if you want a consistent visual system and a CMS structured around that content.

  • Your team needs to update content within clearly defined templates.
  • You want design and hosting in the same platform.
  • You have validated the CMS, forms and integrations needed for your site.
  • The redesign already requires rebuilding pages and reviewing the structure.

Webflow’s official migration guide covers preparing and importing content. An import does not automatically transfer a theme, page builder or plugin logic. Design and functionality need their own plan.

3. When keeping WordPress may be the better decision

A website that works well does not need to move simply because another tool exists. Keeping WordPress can make more sense when your team is comfortable editing it and the site relies on established functionality.

Consider a store with specific pricing rules, a portal with user permissions, courses, custom search or integrations connected to internal processes. Before moving, check how each feature will be reproduced, who will maintain it and what it will cost.

Improving the existing site also deserves a comparison if the problem is concentrated in the design, hosting or a few plugins. A small service website and a platform running complex business processes need different decisions.

A current consideration for membership sites

Webflow retired its native User Accounts feature on January 29, 2026. If you need gated access or member accounts, include an external solution and its maintenance in the evaluation. Read the official notice.

4. Compare everyday work and the total cost

The comparison goes beyond hosting fees. Include the rebuild, content cleanup, licenses or plans, external tools, testing and ongoing support. Check current pricing and limits before approving a budget.

FactorWhat to check
ContentContent types, volume, relationships, languages and required fields.
EditingWho publishes and whether they can complete a real test without assistance.
IntegrationsForms, bookings, CRM, payments and the job each plugin performs.
MaintenanceWho reviews changes, errors, accessibility and external connections.
BudgetMigration costs plus recurring expenses and support.
Future exitWhich data you can export and what you would need to rebuild.

Webflow offers code export under certain conditions, but static exports do not include CMS functionality or all the behavior of a hosted site. Do not treat an export as a complete working copy. Review the export limitations.

5. A migration does not guarantee better SEO

Choosing Webflow does not replace a clear structure, useful content or careful implementation. If addresses change, prepare a URL map and permanent redirects to equivalent pages. Review titles, descriptions, internal links, canonicals, languages, the sitemap and indexing settings.

Google explains that a move involving URL changes can cause fluctuations while pages are crawled and indexed again. Plan a review after launch, without promising that rankings will remain unchanged. Read Google’s site migration guidance.

If you have already decided to move, my website migration checklist helps you organize content, URLs, the CMS and testing before launch.

6. Gather these five things before deciding

  • Your current website link and the three problems you want to solve.
  • An inventory of pages, articles, media and languages.
  • A plugin list with the actual purpose of each plugin.
  • Your available budget for the rebuild and ongoing maintenance.
  • A test of one important page and integration on the proposed platform.

This gives you a basis for comparing a complete migration with improving WordPress. My approach is to choose the option that fits the business and that the team can sustain after launch.

Frequently asked questions

Can I keep my domain?

Yes. A platform change does not require a new domain. The launch plan should address website DNS settings and preserve email records.

Will all my plugins transfer?

WordPress plugins cannot be installed in Webflow. Review what each one does and decide whether to replace it, integrate an external tool or develop an alternative.

How long does a migration take?

It depends on the content, languages, functionality and condition of the current site. A responsible estimate starts with an inventory and a defined scope, rather than the page count alone.
